blocks.c: a team of DC superheroes standing in front of Martian Manhunter in 'Young Justice'

blocks.x: Image via Warner Bros. Animation

Frustrated at being treated like sidekicks, Speedy (Crispin Freeman), Aqualad (Khary Payton), Kid Flash (Jason Spisak), and Robin (Jesse McCartney) investigate a fire at Cadmus Lab and discover that they have made a clone of Superman (Nolan North), called Superboy (North). After freeing Superboy, the Justice League allows the young heroes to form their own team under the League's jurisdiction. They are joined by fellow heroes Miss Martial (Danica McKellar) and Artemis (Stephanie Lemelin), and the team's main source of conflict comes from a mysterious organization called the Light.

Young Justice was co-created by Greg Weisman, one of the creative heads of Disney's Gargoyles, and retains much of the former's fantastic character work and emphasis on strong continuity and character development. The emphasis on sidekicks is also a great premise, as it allows the audience to watch them grow and develop over the seasons: some choose to remain on the team to mentor new heroes, others carve out their own paths, and some come to shocking ends. The show's history is also rather heroic, as it came back from cancelation and jumped between three networks before concluding.

7
'Spider-Man: The Animated Series' (1994–1998)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/spider-man-the-animated-series-black-cat.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Fox Kids Network

After being bitten by a radioactive spider, Peter Parker (Christopher Daniel Barnes) gains super strength, reflexes, and a "Spidey sense" that gives him the ability to sense incoming danger. Using web-shooters, he adopts the persona of Spider-Man to protect the people of New York from criminals, both mundane and superpowered. Unfortunately, this not only earns him plenty of enemies among the criminal underworld, but also forces him to make personal sacrifices in the name of the greater good.

Spider-Man: The Animated Series might suffer from repetitive animation and some of the strangest examples of studio-mandated censorship, but when it's good, it's some of the best storytelling the webhead has ever received. The show adapted classic Spider-Man stories and does a good job balancing Peter's expansive list of side characters, villains, and allies, while not being afraid to try something new. In fact, this show is the origin of several aspects that have become mainstays in Spider-Man canon, such as the Spider-verse.

6
'Invincible' (2021–Presenet)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/invincible-season-2-part-2-mark-grayson-sea-monster.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Mark Grayson fighting a sea monster in Invincible Season 2 Part 2

blocks.x: Image via Prime Video

Upon turning seventeen, Mark Grayson (Steven Yeun) is delighted to develop superpowers and become a superhero like his father, Nolan (J. K. Simmons). As Mark, under the name Invincible, learns the ins and outs of being a superhero, he befriends other heroes his age, such as Atom Eve (Gillian Jacobs), and begins working closely with the Global Defence Agency, headed by Cecil Stedman (Walton Goggins). However, Nolan brutally murders the Guardians of the Globe, Earth's premier superhero team, and as everyone tries to figure out the truth, it leads to shocking revelations and trials of corpses.

Invincible revels in the fact that it is a superhero show and thus pokes fun at and pays homage to the genre's numerous tropes and classic character archetypes. Yet it also uses it as a framing device to tell very mature stories that delve into the mentality of being a superhero, how that responsibility can make or break both the heroes and their loved ones, and how terrifying the world would be if heroes, villains, and monsters were regularly battling one another. The voice cast is phenomenal, with one of the highlights being Sandra Oh as Mark's mother, Deborah, who has to try and be there for Mark while also coming to terms with Nolan's actions.

Four teams, four completely different reasons to put yourself in danger
for strangers. This is the roster you actually belong on, what they would want from you, and what it
would cost you to stay.

Marvel Studios · The Avengers · Since 2012

The Avengers

You belong where the stakes are largest and the personalities are
loudest. This is a team of people who are all used to being the most important person in the
room, which is exactly why it works and exactly why it keeps nearly falling apart.

The Avengers are not friends who became a team. They are a team that slowly and
reluctantly became friends, and you would recognise every stage of that process.

You can hold your own among big egos without needing to win every exchange, which is the
real entry requirement here.

The arguing is part of the method. This group does its best thinking mid-disagreement,
usually at volume, usually in a very expensive building.

When the sky opens, they are who shows up. You would want to be standing in that line.

Marvel · X-Men · Since 1963

The X-Men

You have never had the luxury of being thanked for this. The
X-Men protect a world that has never once been comfortable with them existing, and something
in you understands exactly why they keep doing it anyway.

This is the only team on the list whose central conflict is not a villain. It is being
wanted gone by the same people they keep saving.

You know what it is to be the outsider in a room and to decide, anyway, that you will
not make yourself smaller so everyone else is comfortable.

The X-Men are the most genuine found family in comics. People arrive with nowhere else
to go and are never once asked to explain themselves.

You would not be joining for the glory. There has never been any.

DC · Teen Titans · Since 1964

The Teen Titans

You do not want colleagues, you want your people. The Titans are
the team where the friendship came first and the world-saving turned up afterwards as an
inconvenient side effect.

Every Titan is somebody's sidekick who decided to stop being one. That decision, not the
villain of the week, is what the team is actually about.

You would be joining people who are all working themselves out at the same time as you,
which is far less lonely than being the only one.

The Titans lose regularly. Then they eat together and come back better, which is a more
honest model of growing up than any other team here manages.

The tower would be loud, chaotic, and the first place that ever felt like yours.

Prime Video · The Boys · Since 2019

The Boys

You are not asking who to trust. You worked out the answer a
while ago and it was nobody in a cape. This is where you go once you have decided the people
in charge need watching, and that nobody else is going to do it.

The Boys have no powers, no mandate and no funding. What they have is leverage,
patience, and a very high tolerance for consequences.

You are the person in the room who notices the thing everybody else has quietly agreed
not to mention.

This is not a heroic team and it has never pretended otherwise. It is a group of damaged
people doing necessary work in ways nobody would call clean.

You would not sleep well. You would keep going anyway.

'Young Justice' (2010–2022)

Image via Warner Bros. Animation

Frustrated at being treated like sidekicks, Speedy (Crispin Freeman), Aqualad (Khary Payton), Kid Flash (Jason Spisak), and Robin (Jesse McCartney) investigate a fire at Cadmus Lab and discover that they have made a clone of Superman (Nolan North), called Superboy (North). After freeing Superboy, the Justice League allows the young heroes to form their own team under the League's jurisdiction. They are joined by fellow heroes Miss Martial (Danica McKellar) and Artemis (Stephanie Lemelin), and the team's main source of conflict comes from a mysterious organization called the Light.

Young Justice was co-created by Greg Weisman, one of the creative heads of Disney's Gargoyles, and retains much of the former's fantastic character work and emphasis on strong continuity and character development. The emphasis on sidekicks is also a great premise, as it allows the audience to watch them grow and develop over the seasons: some choose to remain on the team to mentor new heroes, others carve out their own paths, and some come to shocking ends. The show's history is also rather heroic, as it came back from cancelation and jumped between three networks before concluding.

7
'Spider-Man: The Animated Series' (1994–1998)

Image via Fox Kids Network

After being bitten by a radioactive spider, Peter Parker (Christopher Daniel Barnes) gains super strength, reflexes, and a "Spidey sense" that gives him the ability to sense incoming danger. Using web-shooters, he adopts the persona of Spider-Man to protect the people of New York from criminals, both mundane and superpowered. Unfortunately, this not only earns him plenty of enemies among the criminal underworld, but also forces him to make personal sacrifices in the name of the greater good.

Spider-Man: The Animated Series might suffer from repetitive animation and some of the strangest examples of studio-mandated censorship, but when it's good, it's some of the best storytelling the webhead has ever received. The show adapted classic Spider-Man stories and does a good job balancing Peter's expansive list of side characters, villains, and allies, while not being afraid to try something new. In fact, this show is the origin of several aspects that have become mainstays in Spider-Man canon, such as the Spider-verse.

6
'Invincible' (2021–Presenet)

Image via Prime Video

Upon turning seventeen, Mark Grayson (Steven Yeun) is delighted to develop superpowers and become a superhero like his father, Nolan (J. K. Simmons). As Mark, under the name Invincible, learns the ins and outs of being a superhero, he befriends other heroes his age, such as Atom Eve (Gillian Jacobs), and begins working closely with the Global Defence Agency, headed by Cecil Stedman (Walton Goggins). However, Nolan brutally murders the Guardians of the Globe, Earth's premier superhero team, and as everyone tries to figure out the truth, it leads to shocking revelations and trials of corpses.

Invincible revels in the fact that it is a superhero show and thus pokes fun at and pays homage to the genre's numerous tropes and classic character archetypes. Yet it also uses it as a framing device to tell very mature stories that delve into the mentality of being a superhero, how that responsibility can make or break both the heroes and their loved ones, and how terrifying the world would be if heroes, villains, and monsters were regularly battling one another. The voice cast is phenomenal, with one of the highlights being Sandra Oh as Mark's mother, Deborah, who has to try and be there for Mark while also coming to terms with Nolan's actions.
